title: The Necessities and Luxuries of Mate Preferences: Testing the Tradeoffs
author: Norman P. Li, J. Michael Bailey, Douglas T. Kenrick, Joan A. W. Linsenmeier
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(6), 947-955
accessedVia: https://r.jina.ai/ text-extraction proxy over the Semantic Scholar-hosted PDF (fetched with curl, not summarized by an LLM)
notes: PRIMARY target. The mate-dollar/budget-allocation paper. Confirmed via direct full-text extraction (9-page PDF converted to markdown text, all sections present: abstract through conclusion, Tables 1-2 and reference list stripped for raw-01). Studies 1-2 = budget allocation (low/med/high mate-dollar budgets); Study 3 = mate-screening/first-inquiry paradigm. Contains explicit convergence language: 'the sex differences on physical attractiveness and resources decreased as the budget increased' (Study 1) and 'these differences decreased as budget increased' (Study 2), plus General Discussion: 'As budgets increased, women's and men's preferences were more similar, as the sex differences in attractiveness and status diminished.' Also contains the explicit surveys-overstate-pickiness argument in the introduction ('The implicit presumption of sufficiency may lead unconstrained judges to gloss over necessities and emphasize traits that may otherwise be luxuries').

title: Chinese and UK participants' preferences for physical attractiveness and social status in potential mates
author: Lingshan Zhang, Hongyi Wang, Anthony J. Lee, Lisa M. DeBruine, Benedict C. Jones
accessedVia: https://r.jina.ai/ text-extraction proxy over PMC open-access full text (fetched with curl)
notes: Independent replication (University of Glasgow + East China Normal University; preregistered Registered Report, protocol at https://psyarxiv.com/sybp4/, data/code at https://osf.io/rkstx/). No author overlap with Li/Bailey/Kenrick/Linsenmeier. Confirms the necessity/luxury sex-difference architecture (bucket a) in two new cultures using a SINGLE fixed 100-mate-dollar budget per relationship-context condition -- it does NOT vary budget size and therefore provides no test of the low-to-high-budget convergence claim (bucket b). Authors explicitly flag that the Li et al. interaction pattern involving relationship context 'is potentially not robust.'

title: Environmental Influences on Mate Preferences as Assessed by a Scenario Manipulation Experiment
author: Daniele Marzoli, Francesco Moretto, Aura Monti, Ornella Tocci, S. Craig Roberts, Luca Tommasi
accessedVia: https://r.jina.ai/ text-extraction proxy over PMC open-access full text (fetched with curl)
notes: Independent group (Universita G. d'Annunzio, Chieti, Italy + University of Stirling, UK). No author overlap with Li/Bailey/Kenrick/Linsenmeier. Uses a Li-style fixed-budget (120-point) allocation task but manipulates hypothetical ENVIRONMENTAL SCENARIO, not respondent budget size -- so it is only tangential to bucket (b) (convergence-with-budget) and does not test it. Relevant to bucket (a): partially fails to replicate the classic sex difference on economic resources ('we failed to observe the often-reported sex difference according to which women more than men desire partners with economic resources') while replicating the men>women attractiveness difference and the general necessity/luxury trait hierarchy (intelligence > kindness/attractiveness > wealth/dominance/height).

title: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Revisited: Do People Know What They Initially Desire in a Romantic Partner?
author: Paul W. Eastwick, Eli J. Finkel
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(2), 245-264
accessedVia: https://r.jina.ai/ text-extraction proxy over the author's self-hosted PDF (fetched with curl)
notes: Canonical stated-vs-revealed source for bucket (c), as named in the assignment. Northwestern University; not authored by Li/Bailey/Kenrick/Linsenmeier (distinct paradigm: speed-dating, not budget-allocation), though the acknowledgments footnote thanks two of the four Li et al. 2002 co-authors (Bailey, Linsenmeier) for comments -- collegial overlap, not co-authorship or shared method. Reports stated ideal-partner sex differences on physical attractiveness (d=.55) and earning prospects (d=.35) that vanish (both r-differences non-significant, r=.03-.05) when the same participants' actual romantic interest in real speed-dating partners is measured. Note: this paper tests whether STATED ideal preferences predict REVEALED interest in a live-choice setting; it is not a budget-allocation-vs-unconstrained-survey comparison, so it supports the general stated/revealed divergence claim underlying (c) but is not a direct test of Li et al.'s specific 'surveys are free' mechanism (respondents facing zero cost when rating traits one at a time).
